title.en: Pwyll and Arawn: a Year in Annwn
title.zh: 普維爾與阿朗：冥界一年

region.en: Glyn Cuch, Dyved (near Narberth), Pembrokeshire, Wales
region.zh: 威爾斯彭布羅克郡納伯斯附近格林·庫赫谷

texts.period: Recorded in the Red Book of Hergest, c. 1382-1410; Lady Charlotte Guest translation 1849

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1849), 'Pwyll Prince of Dyved', eBook #5160

summary.en: Pwyll, prince of Dyved, sets his dogs on a stag already killed by a pack of white hounds with red ears — the hounds of Annwn; the insulted king Arawn trades shapes with him for a year and a night, and Pwyll, ruling the otherworld in his friend's form and refusing the second blow that once undid Arawn, wins for himself the title Pwyll Pen Annwn, chief of Annwn.
summary.zh: 迪維德親王普維爾縱犬逐已被冥界白身紅耳犬群所殺之牡鹿——此為冥界之犬；受辱之王阿朗與之換形一年一夜；普維爾以阿朗之形治理冥界，拒行昔日使阿朗落敗之第二擊，贏得『冥界之首』之名。

sensitivity.note: Annwn's hounds (white, red-eared) are the standard celtic otherworld color-code; the shape-trade is the founding scene of the Mabinogi's first branch.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849: As Pwyll followed his dogs he lost his companions, and heard the cry of other hounds coming in the opposite direction; in a glade they had brought down a stag, and of all the hounds he had seen in the world he had never seen any like unto these, for their hair was of a brilliant shining white and their ears were red. He drove away those that had brought down the stag and set his own dogs upon it — and a horseman on a large light-grey steed drew near and spoke: 'Chieftain, I know who thou art, and I greet thee not... Greater discourtesy saw I never in man, than to drive away the dogs that were killing the stag and to set upon it thine own.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: The horseman was Arawn, a king of Annwn, and his offer was the shape-trade: 'I will send thee to Annwvyn in my stead, and I will give thee the fairest lady thou didst ever behold to be thy companion, and I will put my form and semblance upon thee... And this shall be for the space of a year from to-morrow, and then we will meet in this place.' One year from that night Arawn was fixed to meet his enemy Havgan, king of Annwvyn, at the ford: 'be thou there in my likeness, and with one stroke that thou givest him, he shall no longer live. And if he ask thee to give him another, give it not, how much soever he may entreat thee, for when I did so, he fought with me next day as well as ever before.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: The year was spent in hunting, minstrelsy and feasting with Arawn's queen — the fairest woman Pwyll had ever beheld — with whom he never lay, but turned his face away night after night, and they talked till morning. At the ford the two kings met alone: at the first thrust the man in Arawn's semblance clove Havgan's shield and helmet and bore him to the ground with a deadly blow. 'What right hast thou to cause my death?... But, for the love of Heaven, since thou hast begun to slay me, complete thy work.' 'Slay thee who may, I will not do so' — and Havgan died of the single stroke, and by noon the next day both kingdoms of Annwn were in Pwyll's power. At Glyn Cuch each took back his own form, and because of the year Pwyll had ruled Annwvyn the prince of Dyved lost his name and was called Pwyll Pen Annwvyn, chief of Annwn, from that time forward. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.

narrative.en:
The first branch of the Mabinogi opens with the smallest possible discourtesy — a hunting etiquette breach — and pays it off with a year in the otherworld: the tale that makes a mortal prince ruler of the land of the dead.

Pwyll, lord of the seven cantrevs of Dyved, was at Narberth his chief palace and minded to hunt in Glyn Cuch. He let loose the dogs, and following them lost his companions — and heard the cry of other hounds coming in the opposite direction, a cry different from his own. In a level glade they brought down a stag, and Pwyll looked not at the stag but at the dogs: of all the hounds he had ever seen he had never seen any like them, for their hair was of a brilliant shining white and their ears were red. And he came toward them, drove off those that had killed the stag, and set his own dogs upon it.

A horseman came up on a large light-grey steed, horn round his neck, clad in grey hunting-wool, and greeted him in the negative: 'Chieftain, I know who thou art, and I greet thee not.' The discourtesy was total and technical: to drive off another man's hounds and set one's own on their kill. 'Though I may not be revenged upon thee, yet I declare to Heaven that I will do thee more dishonour than the value of an hundred stags.' When Pwyll asked how he might redeem the friendship, the stranger named himself: Arawn, a king of Annwn — the otherworld kingdom — and named his enemy: Havgan, another king of Annwn, ever warring against him. And Arawn proposed the shape-trade, the mabinogi's first and greatest bargain: 'I will send thee to Annwvyn in my stead... I will put my form and semblance upon thee, so that not a page of the chamber, nor an officer, nor any other man that has always followed me shall know that it is not I.' For a year and a night. Pwyll asked only what would become of his own kingdom; Arawn answered that no one in Dyved would know he was not Pwyll.

So the year passed — hunting, minstrelsy, feasting — and with one exception that the tale watches closely: Arawn's queen, the fairest woman Pwyll had ever beheld, lay beside him every night, and every night he turned his back and face away, and they talked till morning. Friendship kept, honor kept — the tale is measuring Pwyll for kingship.

At the year's end came the ford. A knight arose: 'It is between two kings that this meeting is... do all of you stand aside and leave the fight to be between them.' At the first thrust the man in Arawn's semblance clove Havgan's shield and helmet and bore him an arm's and a spear's length over the crupper of his horse. 'What right hast thou to cause my death? I was not injuring thee in anything... But, for the love of Heaven, since thou hast begun to slay me, complete thy work.' And Pwyll refused — 'slay thee who may, I will not do so' — knowing that the second blow had been Arawn's undoing: the stroke that Havgan had asked of him was the stroke that had renewed Havgan each time he gave it. Havgan died of the one stroke; the nobles submitted; and by noon the next day both kingdoms of Annwn were in Pwyll's power.

At Glyn Cuch they met and each took back his own form. Arawn found his household unknowing of any absence; Pwyll found his people praising a wisdom, kindness and justice they had never seen in him before. He told them the truth, and they said: render thanks to Heaven that thou hast such a fellowship. And by reason of that year — and of uniting the two kingdoms in one day by his valor — Pwyll lost the name of Pwyll Prince of Dyved, and was called Pwyll Pen Annwvyn, chief of Annwn, from that time forward. The otherworld had tested him with a bed he would not sleep in and a stroke he would not give, and given him a title no other mortal holds.
narrative.zh: 馬比諾吉第一支以最小的失禮開篇——一樁狩獵禮儀之失——而以彼岸之一年償付：此篇使一凡俗親王成為冥土之主。迪維德七郡之主普維爾居納伯斯主宮、欲獵於格林·庫赫谷。縱犬逐獸、失其同伴——而聞另一犬群之吠聲自相反方向而來。平坦林間空地上，彼等擊倒一牡鹿；普維爾不視鹿而視犬：生平所見獵犬無一與之相似——毛為光耀之白、耳為紅色。他趨前驅開殺鹿之犬、縱己犬於其上。一騎士乘淺灰巨駿而來，頸掛號角、衣灰色獵服，以否定的方式問候：『首領，我識得你，而不向你問好。』失禮乃技術性的全然：驅他人之犬、縱己犬於其獵物。『我雖不能向你復仇，然我向天宣示：我將予你百鹿之價以上之羞辱。』普維爾問如何贖回誼；異客自名：阿朗，冥界（Annwn）之王——並名其敵：哈夫岡，另一冥界之王，與他長年交戰。阿朗遂提議換形——馬比諾吉之第一且最偉大之交易：『我將遣你代我入冥界……我將加我之形貌於你，使我宮中侍童、官員、乃至常隨之人無一人知其非我。』為期一年一夜。普維爾惟問其本國如何；阿朗答：迪維德無人知其非普維爾。於是為期一年——狩獵、樂事、宴飲——而有一例外為故事密切注視：阿朗之后、普維爾平生所見最美之婦人，每夜與之同榻，而他每夜背身轉面、與之言談至天明。友誼得守、名節得守——此篇正在為王位稱量普維爾。歲末至渡口。一騎士起立：『此乃二王之會……爾等皆退、留二人獨鬥。』首次交擊，代阿朗之形者劈裂哈夫岡之盾與盔、將其擊落馬後一臂一矛之距。『你有何權致我死命？我未傷你分毫……既已傷我，求天之下，將我殺死、成全此事。』而普維爾拒之——『能殺你者我亦不殺』——因知昔日哈夫岡所求於阿朗之第二擊，正是每次使哈夫岡復原之擊。哈夫岡死於單擊；群臣臣服；翌日正午，冥界二國盡入普維爾之手。格林·庫赫重逢，各復己形。阿朗歸而見家人對其離去一無所覺；普維爾歸而其民稱頌前所未有之智慧、仁慈與公義。他講出真相，眾人曰：感謝上天賜你此誼。因那一年——及其一日之內以勇武聯合二國之功——普維爾失『迪維德親王』之名，自彼時起被稱為普維爾·佩恩·安努文，冥界之首。彼岸以一張他不受之床與一擊他不肯出之劍試驗了他，而授予凡人所未曾有之頭銜。

functions: Charter of otherworld sovereignty: a mortal earns the title 'chief of Annwn' by honoring boundaries
Theological color-code: white bodies, red ears as the otherworld hounds of Annwn (later Cŵn Annwn)
Geis-structure of the second blow: the refusal to repeat the stroke as covenant keeping
Hospitality law: the year in Annwn as trial of the guest who must not touch his host's wife

title.en: The Lady on the White Horse and the Badger in the Bag

region.zh: 威爾斯彭布羅克郡納伯斯阿伯斯·阿貝斯王丘

texts.period: Recorded in the Red Book of Hergest, c. 1382-1410; Lady Charlotte Guest translation 1849

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1849), 'Pwyll Prince of Dyved', eBook #5160

summary.en: On the mound of Gorsedd Arberth a lady on a slow white horse passes pursuers who can never close the distance; Pwyll calls out her own words and she stops — Rhiannon, fleeing a marriage she does not want — but a rash boon given at the feast hands her to Gwawl, until she engineers the bag: however much is put in it never fills, until the man of wealth treads it down, and the game of Badger-in-the-Bag is played for the first time.
summary.zh: 阿伯斯王丘上，一白馬女子緩行而來、任何追者永不能縮短距離；普維爾以其自己的話呼之，她停步——這是萊安儂，逃離不願之婚約——但宴上輕許之諾把她讓給瓜爾；她設袋之計：袋中無論放入多少永不滿，直至富有之人踏之，『袋中獾』遊戲首次上演。

sensitivity.note: Rhiannon's white horse and slow pace mark her as a sovereignty/horse-goddess figure; the mound of Gorsedd Arberth carries its own rule — whoever sits on it gets wounds or a wonder.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849: Pwyll went to the top of a mound above his palace called Gorsedd Arberth, though a courtier warned that 'whosoever sits upon it cannot go thence, without either receiving wounds or blows, or else seeing a wonder.' While he sat they saw a lady on a pure white horse of large size, with a garment of shining gold, coming along the highway; and the horse moved at a slow and even pace. A rider on foot followed her, and the greater his speed the further she was from him; a horse and the swiftest in the realm followed her, and still the more he urged his horse the further was she from him, yet she held the same pace as at first. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: On the third day Pwyll himself rode after her and called, 'O maiden, for the sake of him whom thou best lovest, stay for me.' 'I will stay gladly, and it were better for thy horse hadst thou asked it long since.' She was Rhiannon, daughter of Heveydd Hen: 'they sought to give me to a husband against my will. But no husband would I have, and that because of my love for thee... And hither have I come to hear thy answer.' She bade him meet her in a year at the palace of Heveydd, where a feast would be prepared. At the feast a tall auburn-haired youth entered and asked as his boon the lady Pwyll loved best — Gwawl son of Clud, the very man Rhiannon was fleeing — and Pwyll's rash answer bound him. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Rhiannon set the stratagem of the bag: 'See that thou keep it well... I will cause that if all the meat and liquor that are in these seven Cantrevs were put into it, it would be no fuller than before... Say thou then that it never will, until a man of noble birth and of great wealth arise and press the food in the bag with both his feet, saying, Enough has been put therein.' A year later Pwyll came in ragged garments with the bag, asked only a bagful of food, and the more was put in the emptier it stayed; Gwawl rose and trod the food down — 'and Pwyll turned up the sides of the bag, so that Gwawl was over his head in it.

passages.text: And he shut it up quickly and slipped a knot upon the thongs, and blew his horn.' His hundred knights came down and every one struck a blow upon the bag, asking 'What is here?' 'A Badger' — 'The game of Badger in the Bag' — and thus was the game of Badger in the Bag first played. Gwawl was spared for sureties and gifts to suitors and minstrels, and never sought revenge. Not verbatim.

narrative.en:
The second movement of Pwyll's mabinogi is a courtship conducted on a mound with its own law, and resolved by the earliest game in Welsh literature.

Pwyll was at Narberth, his chief palace, where a feast had been prepared, and after the first meal he arose to walk — to the top of a mound above the palace called Gorsedd Arberth. A courtier warned him of the mound's peculiarity: 'whosoever sits upon it cannot go thence, without either receiving wounds or blows, or else seeing a wonder.' 'I fear not to receive wounds and blows in the midst of such a host as this, but as to the wonder, gladly would I see it.' So he sat upon the mound — and the wonder came riding toward him: a lady on a pure white horse of large size, in a garment of shining gold, at a slow and even pace. One of his men followed her on foot, and the greater his speed the further she was from him; the next day the swiftest horse in the realms followed her and could not close the gap; she held always the same pace. On the third day Pwyll rode after her himself — and when the horse failed, he did what no pursuer had done: he used words. 'O maiden, for the sake of him whom thou best lovest, stay for me.' 'I will stay gladly,' said she, 'and it were better for thy horse hadst thou asked it long since.' The riddle of the slow pursuit is the tale's theology: the sovereignty-goddess cannot be overtaken by force or wealth, only addressed.

She threw back her head-dress and fixed her eyes on him; and the beauty of all the maidens he had ever seen was as nothing compared to her. 'My chief quest was to seek thee,' said Rhiannon, daughter of Heveydd Hen: they sought to give her to a husband against her will, but no husband would she have because of her love for Pwyll. She set the tryst: this day twelvemonth, at the palace of Heveydd, with the feast prepared.

At the feast, in the middle of the carousal, a tall auburn-haired youth of royal bearing entered and claimed his boon — the lady whom Pwyll loved best, 'with the feast and the banquet that are in this place' — and Pwyll, whose wits the Mabinogi constantly tests, had already answered 'What boon soever thou mayest ask of me, as far as I am able, thou shalt have.' The suitor was Gwawl son of Clud — the very man Rhiannon had fled. 'Never did man make worse use of his wits than thou hast done,' said Rhiannon; and she laid the counter-plot herself. 'In thy hand will I give thee a small bag... I will cause that if all the meat and liquor that are in these seven Cantrevs were put into it, it would be no fuller than before... Say thou then that it never will, until a man of noble birth and of great wealth arise and press the food in the bag with both his feet, saying, Enough has been put therein.'

A year to the night, Pwyll came to the feast in coarse ragged garments and clumsy old shoes, asking nothing but a bagful of food for his need. Attendants filled the bag, and for all they put into it it was no fuller than at first; the seven cantrevs' meat and liquor went in and the bag stayed empty; and Gwawl, at Rhiannon's prompt, rose and trod the food down with both feet. 'And Pwyll turned up the sides of the bag, so that Gwawl was over his head in it. And he shut it up quickly and slipped a knot upon the thongs, and blew his horn' — the hundred knights came down from the orchard and took the host. Every knight that entered struck a blow on the bag and asked 'What is here?' 'A Badger,' said they; and so they played, each striking it with foot or staff, and thus was the game of Badger in the Bag first played. The bagged man asked not to die in a bag; Heveydd and Rhiannon counseled mercy — let him satisfy the suitors and minstrels in Pwyll's place, with sureties never to seek revenge. Pwyll wedded Rhiannon, and Gwawl's household in the otherworld kept the account: the mabinogi's later enchantment of Dyved will be billed to the Badger in the Bag.
narrative.zh: 普維爾馬比諾吉之第二樂章，是一場於帶法之丘上進行、並以威爾斯文學中最早之遊戲化解之求婚。普維爾居納伯斯主宮，初餐之後起身而行——登上宮上名為阿伯斯·阿貝斯之丘。廷臣警告此丘之特性：『凡坐其上者，非受傷受擊不得離去，或必見奇觀。』『於此等眾人中我不怕受傷受擊，至於奇觀，我樂於一見。』他坐於丘上——奇觀騎馬而來：一女子乘純白巨馬、披光耀金衣、緩步均速而來。其一人徒步追之，愈追愈遠；翌日全境最快之馬追之，距離如故；她始終保持同一速度。第三日普維爾親自乘馬追之——當馬力竭，他做了所有追者未做之事：用語言。『姑娘，為你最愛者之故，為我停留。』『我樂於停留——你若早說，你的馬也不至於此。』緩行追逐之謎即此篇之神學：主權女神不能被武力或財富追上，只能以言語召喚。她掀開面紗、定睛看他；他所見過的一切美女之美與她相比皆為烏有。『我此行主要為尋你，』希維德·亨之女萊安儂曰：族中欲違其願將她許嫁，而她因愛普維爾不從。她定約：一年後之今日，於希維德宮中相會，宴席已備。宴中行樂之際，一高挑紅髮王儀之青年入廳索取其諾——普維爾最愛之女子『與此地之宴與酒』——而普維爾早已答過『你所能求者，凡我能給者必予』。求婚者乃瓜爾·克魯德之子——即萊安儂所逃之人。『從無男子比你的機智用得更糟，』萊安儂曰；並親自定下反計。『我將一小袋交於你手……七郡之肉與酒縱然盡入其中，亦不比先前更滿……你當答曰：永不會滿，除非一位有田產財富之貴人起身以雙足踏實袋中之食，並說：已放足了。』一年後之是夜，普維爾著襤褸舊履而來，所求不過一袋之食。侍從填袋，愈填愈空；七郡之肉酒盡入而袋如故；瓜爾應萊安儂之催促起身、以雙足踏實其食。『普維爾翻起袋緣，使瓜爾沒頂其中。他迅速束緊袋帶、打了結、吹響號角』——百騎自果園直下、擒其從眾。每位入場騎士各擊袋一記問『此為何物？』『是一隻獾』——『袋中獾之戲』——袋中獾之戲遂首次上演。袋中人求勿死於袋中；希維德與萊安儂主寬——令其在普維爾之位上款待求婚者與吟遊詩人，並具保永不復仇。普維爾娶萊安儂；而彼岸瓜爾之族記下此帳：馬比諾吉後文迪維德之魔咒，帳單正開向袋中獾。

functions: Sovereignty-goddess courtship: the bride who can only be addressed, never overtaken
Etiology of the game 'Badger in the Bag' — a ritualized humiliation of the failed suitor
The mound's law (wounds or a wonder): Gorsedd Arberth as an oracle-seat
Legal doctrine of the rash boon: a promise given before the nobles binds the king

summary.en: Six watchwomen sleep through the night the heir of Dyved is born, then frame Rhiannon for devouring her own son — blood of puppies on her face and hands; she chooses penance over contention and sits seven years by the horseblock offering to carry guests into the palace, while on Gwent the stolen boy arrives in the same May-night claw that has taken every colt, and Teirnyon finds an infant in satin where the foal should have been.
summary.zh: 迪維德繼承人誕生之夜，六名守望婦女酣睡，事後誣萊安儂食其親子——以幼犬之血塗其面手；她選擇贖罪而非爭辯，於馬石旁坐七年、願背訪客入宮；同時在格溫特，被竊之嬰於五月之夜爪中抵達——特尼昂於本應得駒之處發現緞衣嬰孩。

sensitivity.note: The May-eve claw and the vanished foals are the Welsh mabinogi's version of the changeling/sacred-birth complex; Rhiannon's penance is the famous 'I will carry them on my back' image.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849: Before the end of a year a son was born to Pwyll and Rhiannon at Narberth, and on the night that he was born six women were brought to watch the mother and the boy; before midnight every one of them fell asleep, and towards break of day they awoke and looked where they had put the boy, and behold he was not there. One counselled: 'There is here a stag-hound bitch, and she has a litter of whelps. Let us kill some of the cubs, and rub the blood on the face and hands of Rhiannon, and lay the bones before her, and assert that she herself hath devoured her son, and she alone will not be able to gainsay us six.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Rhiannon asked only for the truth, promising to defend them if they feared; the women held to their lie, and the story went throughout the land, and the nobles besought Pwyll to put away his wife. He answered that they had no cause save her having no children: 'But children has she now had, therefore will I not put her away; if she has done wrong, let her do penance for it.' The penance was that she should remain at Narberth to the end of seven years, sit every day near the horseblock without the gate, tell the story to all who came, and offer to carry guests and strangers on her back into the palace — but it rarely happened that any would permit. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Teirnyon Twryv Vliant of Gwent Is Coed had a mare that foaled on the night of every first of May and whose colts always vanished; he armed and watched, and the mare foaled a large colt — then a claw came through the window and seized it by the mane, and Teirnyon struck off the arm at the elbow; tumult and wailing followed, and rushing out he came back to find at his door an infant boy in swaddling-clothes wrapped in a mantle of satin, very strong for his age. His wife called him Gwri Wallt Euryn for his gold hair; he grew faster than any child, and was given the colt saved the night he was found. Hearing of Rhiannon's punishment, Teirnyon saw in the boy a great likeness to Pwyll, went to Narberth, and refused the offered back: 'Think not that I will be one to be carried upon thy back.' At the feast he restored the boy — 'and whosoever told that lie concerning thee, has done wrong' — and Pendaran Dyved named him Pryderi, from the word his mother spoke when she received the joyful tidings. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.

narrative.en:
The birth of Pryderi is the Mabinogi's darkest domestic scene and its tenderest restoration: a queen libeled for cannibalism, a penance of patience, and a stolen child returned by the very claw that steals colts.

For two years Pwyll and Rhiannon ruled prosperously, and in the third the nobles grew sorrowful at having no heir. Pwyll asked a year; before it was out a son was born at Narberth, and on the night of his birth six women were brought to watch the mother and the boy. Before midnight every one of them slept, and toward break of day they awoke and the boy was not there. And they took counsel: 'There is here a stag-hound bitch, and she has a litter of whelps. Let us kill some of the cubs, and rub the blood on the face and hands of Rhiannon, and lay the bones before her, and assert that she herself hath devoured her son, and she alone will not be able to gainsay us six.' Rhiannon, waking, asked only where her son was; they told her she had struggled with them violently — 'hast thou not thyself devoured thy son?' She promised to defend them if they spoke from fear; they held to the lie. The story went through the land, the nobles besought Pwyll to put her away, and Pwyll answered with the law: they had no cause but childlessness, 'but children has she now had, therefore will I not put her away; if she has done wrong, let her do penance for it.'

Rhiannon chose penance over contention, and the penance was seven years at Narberth: every day she sat near the horse-block outside the gate, told her own story to strangers, and offered to carry them into the palace on her back — 'but it rarely happened that any would permit.' The great queen who rode a slow white horse past all pursuers now sits at a mounting-block waiting to carry men: the sovereignty of the land turned upside down by six liars.

Meanwhile in Gwent Is Coed, Teirnyon Twryv Vliant kept a mare than which none in the kingdom was more beautiful — and on the night of every first of May she foaled, and no one ever knew what became of the colt. One May night Teirnyon armed himself and watched. The mare foaled a large and beautiful colt; then he heard a great tumult, and a claw came through the window and seized the colt by the mane; Teirnyon drew his sword and struck off the arm at the elbow, so that the arm and the colt were in the house with him. Tumult and wailing followed; he rushed out after the noise — and remembered he had left the door open — and returned to find at his door an infant boy in swaddling-clothes, wrapped in a mantle of satin, and very strong for his age. His wife, who had never had a child, took the boy and feigned pregnancy; they baptized him Gwri Wallt Euryn, for the hair on his head was as yellow as gold, and he grew faster than any child in the world — at a year old he walked stoutly, before his fourth year he was bribing grooms to let him water the horses. And the colt, saved the night he was found, was broken in and given to the boy: each the twin of the other's deliverance.

When Teirnyon heard the tale of Rhiannon's penance, he looked steadfastly on the boy and saw the greatest likeness between father and son he had ever beheld — for he had of old been Pwyll's follower. Grieved at keeping another man's son while so excellent a lady was punished, he rode to Narberth with two knights, and Rhiannon rose beside the horse-block: 'go not further thus, I will bear every one of you into the palace, and this is my penance for slaying my own son and devouring him.' 'Oh, fair lady,' said Teirnyon, 'think not that I will be one to be carried upon thy back.' 'Neither will I,' said the boy. At the feast Teirnyon set the boy before Rhiannon: 'And behold here is thy son, lady. And whosoever told that lie concerning thee, has done wrong.' Pendaran Dyved gave the name: Pryderi — 'care, anxiety' — from the word his mother spoke when she received the joyful tidings; and thus ended the penance of Rhiannon and the secret nursling of Gwent.
narrative.zh: 普里德里誕生乃馬比諾吉最黑暗之家庭場景與最溫柔之復和：一位被誣食人的王后、一場以耐心行之贖罪、以及一個由偷駒之爪親手送回的被竊嬰孩。普維爾與萊安儂興治兩年；第三年貴族憂無嗣。普維爾求一年；未及滿年一子誕於納伯斯，誕生之夜六名婦女受命守護母子。午夜前人人入睡；天將明醒來，嬰孩不見。她們合謀：『此處有獵犬母犬及其幼犬。殺數隻幼犬、以血塗萊安儂之面與手、置骨於其前、堅稱她親自食其子——她一人無法反駁我們六人。』萊安儂醒來只問兒子何在；她們答其曾暴力掙扎——『你豈非自己食了兒子？』她許諾若因懼而說則必護她們；她們堅持謊言。消息傳遍全境，貴族請普維爾休妻，普維爾以法答之：除無子外別無理由休妻——『而今她有子，故我不休她；若她有過，令其贖罪。』萊安儂擇贖罪而非爭辯：納伯斯七年，每日坐於門外馬石旁、向來客講述自己的故事、並願背訪客入宮——『然極少有人允許。』曾騎白馬勝過一切追逐者的偉大女王，如今坐於上馬石旁等待背負男子：六名說謊者把土地的主權翻了過來。同時在格溫特伊斯科德，特尼昂·圖里夫·弗利安特畜一匹王國最美的母馬——每年五月朔夜產駒、而駒總是消失。一夜特尼昂披甲守候。母馬產下一匹大而美的駒；隨即他聞巨響，一爪自窗入、抓住駒鬣；特尼昂拔劍自肘部斬落其臂——斷臂與駒皆在屋內。喧嚷與哀哭隨之；他循聲衝出——記起門未關——回來時門邊有一襁褓嬰孩、裹緞衣、體力遠超其齡。從未育子的妻子收下男嬰、佯稱懷孕；為其洗禮命名格維·瓦爾特·尤林，因其髮黃如金；其成長快過世上任何孩童——一歲穩步、四歲前已賄馬伕牽馬飲水。而被救之夜所產之駒經馴後賜予此孩：各為彼此解救之雙生。特尼昂聞萊安儂贖罪之事，凝視男孩、見生平所未見之父子相似——因他昔日曾是普維爾隨從。為另一人之子而令賢后受罰，他不忍，遂偕二騎至納伯斯；萊安儂起身於馬石旁：『莫再前行，我願背爾等入宮，此乃我食親子之贖罪。』『美后，』特尼昂曰，『我斷不會讓你背負。』『我也不會，』男孩曰。宴上特尼昂置男孩於萊安儂前：『看，這是你的兒子，夫人。凡造此謊者，行不義。』彭達蘭·迪維德命名：普里德里——『憂念』——出自其母得喜訊時所說之詞；萊安儂之贖罪與格溫特之密養至此終結。

functions: The theology of false accusation: choosing penance over dispute as a display of sovereignty's dignity
Changeling/night-raid birth myth: the May-eve claw that takes foals and delivers a prince
Fosterage law dramatized: Teirnyon's restitution with three gains (thanks, gifts, a foster-son)
Etiology of Pryderi's name from the mother's word of joyful care

title.en: Branwen, the Cauldron of Rebirth and the Warring of Two Islands
title.zh: 布蘭溫、再生之釜與二島之戰

region.en: Aberffraw, Anglesey, Wales (wedding seat of the alliance)
region.zh: 威爾斯安格爾西島阿伯弗勞（聯姻之地）

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1849), 'Branwen the Daughter of Llyr', eBook #5160

summary.en: Matholwch king of Ireland weds Branwen to league Ireland with the Island of the Mighty; Evnissyen mutilates the wedding horses, the insult is paid with horses and the cauldron of rebirth, and still the foster-brothers dishonor Branwen — cook and daily blow on the ear — until she teaches a starling to carry her letter across the sea, and Brân walks the ocean with his fleet as a wood on the water.
summary.zh: 愛爾蘭王馬索爾奇娶布蘭溫以聯盟二島；埃文尼森殘害婚馬，以馬匹與再生之釜賠罪，而其乳兄弟仍辱布蘭溫——命其烹飪、每日批頰一記——直至她訓練椋鳥攜書渡海，白蘭徒步渡洋、其艦隊如海上之林。

sensitivity.note: The cauldron of rebirth (reviving the dead but mute) is the Mabinogi's central resurrection technology; the starling-letter is the cycle's most famous message-device.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849: Matholwch king of Ireland sailed thirteen ships to Harlech to ask Branwen the daughter of Llyr, one of the three chief ladies of the island, that the Island of the Mighty might be leagued with Ireland. She was wedded to him at Aberffraw. But Evnissyen, the half-brother who would cause strife between his brothers when they were most at peace, 'rushed under the horses and cut off their lips at the teeth, and their ears close to their heads, and their tails close to their backs, and wherever he could clutch their eyelids, he cut them to the very bone, and he disfigured the horses and rendered them useless.' Matholwch left in anger, and atonements were made: a sound horse for every horse injured, a staff of silver as large and tall as himself, a plate of gold of the breadth of his face — and Branwen's counsel added the cauldron: 'the property of which is, that if one of thy men be slain to-day, and be cast therein, to-morrow he will be as well as ever he was at the best, except that he will not regain his speech.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: In Ireland the foster-brothers of Matholwch rose in tumult over the insult, and the vengeance they took was 'to drive away Branwen from the same chamber with him, and to make her cook for the Court; and they caused the butcher after he had cut up the meat to come to her and give her every day a blow on the ear.' Ships and ferries were forbidden to Cambria for three years, that the thing be not known there. Branwen reared a starling in the cover of the kneading-trough, taught it to speak and to know her brother, wrote a letter of her woes and bound it to the root of the bird's wing; it found Brân at Caer Seiont in Arvon and alighted on his shoulder. He summoned sevenscore and four countries and sailed for Ireland — and his host appeared to the swineherds as a wood upon the sea, a mountain moving beside it, with a ridge between two lakes: the fleet's masts, Brân wading to the shore, and his two eyes wroth. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: The Irish broke the bridge over the Llinon and Brân said: 'he who will be chief, let him be a bridge. I will be so' — and lay down across the river, hurdles upon him, the host passing over. Peace was made in a great house built to contain him; but the Irish had hung leathern bags on each side of the hundred pillars with an armed man in each, and Evnissyen went the rounds feeling the bags — 'Meal, good soul' — and crushed every hidden head but one. At the peace feast he seized the boy Gwern by the feet and thrust him into the blazing fire; Branwen strove to leap in after her son, and Brân grasped her between shield and shoulder.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Irish kindled fire under the cauldron of renovation and cast their dead into it, and next day they came forth fighting-men as good as before, except that they could not speak. Evnissyen, seeing the men of the Island of the Mighty nowhere resuscitated, cast himself among the Irish dead, and was flung into the cauldron — and he stretched himself out in it and rent it into four pieces, and burst his own heart also. Only seven men of the Island of the Mighty escaped, and Brân himself was wounded in the foot with a poisoned dart. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.

narrative.en:
The second branch of the Mabinogi is the great Irish-Welsh war tale — a marriage that becomes a massacre, saved at last by a cauldron that revives the dead and a heart too great to survive its own guilt.

Brân the Blessed, son of Llyr, crowned king of the island and too large for any house, sat at Harlech looking over the sea with his brother Manawyddan and the two sons of his mother — Nissyen, who made peace between his kindred even when their wrath was highest, and Evnissyen, who made strife between his brothers when they were most at peace. Thirteen ships came from Ireland bearing Matholwch, suitor for Branwen the daughter of Llyr, one of the three chief ladies of the island: the league of Ireland and the Island of the Mighty. They wedded her at Aberffraw, under tents, for no house could contain Brân.

Next day Evnissyen found the Irish horses and asked whose they were — his sister's husband's. 'And is it thus they have done with a maiden such as she, and moreover my sister, bestowing her without my consent? They could have offered no greater insult to me than this.' And he rushed under the horses and cut off their lips at the teeth, their ears close to their heads, their tails close to their backs, and their eyelids to the very bone — leaving the alliance's cavalry useless. Matholwch left in anger: 'the insult was not done me before they had bestowed upon me a maiden so exalted as she.' Brân sent embassies with atonements: a sound horse for every horse injured, a staff of silver as large and tall as Matholwch himself, a plate of gold of the breadth of his face — and, at Branwen's own counsel, the cauldron: 'I will give unto thee a cauldron, the property of which is, that if one of thy men be slain to-day, and be cast therein, to-morrow he will be as well as ever he was at the best, except that he will not regain his speech.' The cauldron came to Matholwch from Llassar Llaesgyvnewid, the giant who had escaped the red-hot Iron House of Ireland — an origin story that seeds the war to come.

In Ireland Branwen bore Matholwch a son, Gwern, and spent a year in honor — until the foster-brothers rose in tumult over the old insult, and took their vengeance on her: 'to drive away Branwen from the same chamber with him, and to make her cook for the Court; and they caused the butcher after he had cut up the meat to come to her and give her every day a blow on the ear.' For three years every ship and ferry was forbidden to Cambria that the thing not be known there. So Branwen reared a starling in the kneading-trough's cover, taught it speech and the appearance of her brother, wrote her woes in a letter bound beneath its wing, and sent it toward Britain; it found Brân at Caer Seiont, alighted on his shoulder and ruffled its feathers till the letter showed. Brân summoned sevenscore and four countries, leaving seven men to guard the island under Caradawc. The Irish saw a wood upon the sea where no tree had ever been: the masts and yards of ships; a mountain moving beside it with a ridge and two lakes: Brân wading to the shore, his two eyes wroth.

The Irish broke the bridge over the river Llinon; Brân said, 'he who will be chief, let him be a bridge. I will be so' — and lay himself across the river, hurdles upon him, the host passing over, and that saying first uttered, used as a proverb since. Peace was made in a house built to contain him for the first time in his life; the Irish hung a leathern bag on each of the hundred pillars, an armed man in each — and Evnissyen went the rounds asking 'What is in this bag?' 'Meal, good soul' — feeling the heads within and crushing them one by one, leaving but a single life. Then, at the feast, he seized the boy Gwern by the feet — the boy beloved by all who beheld him, called from uncle to uncle in love — and thrust him headlong into the blazing fire; Branwen strove to leap into the fire after her son, and Brân grasped her between his shield and his shoulder.

The battle of the house followed, and its secret weapon: the Irish kindled fire under the cauldron of renovation and cast their dead bodies into it until it was full, and next day the dead came forth fighting-men as good as before — except that they could not speak. The men of the Island of the Mighty were killed and not revived. And Evnissyen, who began it all, saw that his people were nowhere resuscitated, and said in his heart: 'Alas! woe is me, that I should have been the cause of bringing the men of the Island of the Mighty into so great a strait. Evil betide me if I find not a deliverance therefrom.' He cast himself among the dead bodies of the Irish; two unshod Irishmen, taking him for one of their own dead, flung him into the cauldron; and he stretched himself out in it and rent it into four pieces, bursting his own heart also — the resurrection machine broken from within by the man who lit the war. Only seven escaped with Brân, himself wounded in the foot with a poisoned dart.
narrative.zh: 馬比諾吉第二支乃偉大的愛爾蘭-威爾斯戰爭之篇——一樁婚姻成為屠殺，最後由一釜能起死回生之器與一顆無法承載自身罪責之心拯救。白蘭（Bendigeid Vran）、裡爾之子、海島加冕之王、巨軀無屋可容，坐於哈利克海崖上，偕弟瑪南南與其母之二子——最怒時也能使親族和好之內西恩，與最和時也使兄弟相爭之埃文尼森。十三艘船自愛爾蘭而來，載馬索爾奇——為求娶裡爾之女布蘭溫、全島三貴女之一——以結愛爾蘭與巨人島之盟。二人在阿伯弗勞成婚——於帳篷之下，因無屋可容白蘭。次日埃文尼森遇愛爾蘭馬群，問屬誰——其妹夫之馬。『他們竟如此對待一位如此尊貴、且為我妹之女子，未經我同意便許嫁——世間無大於此之辱。』他衝入馬群之下，削其唇及齒、削耳至根、削尾至臀、眼瞼削至骨——聯盟騎兵盡廢。馬索爾奇憤而離去；白蘭遣使賠罪：每傷一馬償一健馬、白銀杖高長如其身、金版寬如其面——且依布蘭溫之策，加上那口釜：『我予你一釜，其性為：若你之人今日被殺、投入其中，明日便如昔日全盛之時——只是不能復言。』此釜來自愛爾蘭赤熱鐵屋中逃生之巨人拉薩爾——為將來之戰播種。在愛爾蘭，布蘭溫生子格溫恩、一年享尊榮——直至馬索爾奇之乳兄弟為舊辱生亂，向她報復：『將布蘭溫逐出其室、令她為王庭烹飪；屠夫分割肉塊後須每日至她處批頰一記。』三年之中船渡皆禁行康布利亞以防消息外洩。於是布蘭溫在揉面槽蓋中養一椋鳥、教其言語與其兄之形貌、將其苦難寫成書信繫於鳥翼之根、送往不列顛；鳥於阿爾方凱爾·塞翁特尋得白蘭、落其肩、梳羽至信現。白蘭召集七國十四部，留七人守島、以卡拉多克為首。愛爾蘭人於從未見樹之海上見一森林——乃艦隊之桅與帆；其旁一移動之山、脊上二湖：白蘭涉水而來、雙目含怒。愛爾蘭人斷河上之橋；白蘭曰：『為首者，當為橋。我便是。』遂臥於河上、其上加籬、大軍渡之——此語首次說出、自彼時成為諺語。和議於一座生平首次能容他的大屋中締結；愛爾蘭人在百柱兩側各懸皮袋、各藏一甲士——埃文尼森巡問『袋中何物？』『上好麵粉，好人』——逐一捏碎袋中之頭，僅餘一命。和宴之上，他抓起男孩格溫恩之足——那為所有見者所愛、被叔伯輪流呼喚的男孩——倒舉投入烈火；布蘭溫欲躍入火中隨子，白蘭以盾與肩夾住她。屋戰隨起，其秘密武器為：愛爾蘭人在再生之釜下生火、投入死屍至滿，翌日死者如前復出為戰士——只是不能言語。巨人島之人被殺而不得復生。始作俑者埃文尼森見族人無一復生，心中曰：『禍哉！我竟使巨人島之人陷此絕境。若不得解救，願禍臨我。』他投身愛爾蘭死者之間；兩名赤足愛爾蘭人誤認其為己族之屍、投入釜中；他在釜中伸展其軀、將釜裂為四片、亦迸裂己心——點燃戰火之人自內毀壞復活之器。僅七人與白蘭逃脫，其足亦中毒鏢。

summary.en: Wounded in the foot by a poisoned dart, Brân commands his seven survivors to cut off his head and bear it to the White Mount in London, face to France — seven years feasting at Harlech with the birds of Rhiannon, eighty years in the hall at Gwales with two doors open and the third closed, until Heilyn opens the forbidden door and all their sorrows return at once; the buried head guards the island from invasion as long as it lies there.
summary.zh: 足中毒鏢的白蘭命七位倖存者斬其首、攜往倫敦白丘面向法蘭西而葬——在哈利克七年宴飲、萊安儂之鳥歌唱；於格瓦勒斯廳八十年、二門開而第三門閉——直至海林開禁門、眾悲瞬間湧回；其頭埋於白丘期間，海島免受外海入侵。

sensitivity.note: The head as national talisman parallels the Welsh tradition of the head-cult (cf. the Celtic 'cult of the head'); the third 'ill-fated disclosure' motif frames British history as burial-and-exhumation.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849: Only seven men of the Island of the Mighty escaped — Pryderi, Manawyddan, Gluneu Eil Taran, Taliesin, Ynawc, Grudyen son of Muryel, and Heilyn son of Gwynn Hen — and Brân himself was wounded in the foot with a poisoned dart. And Brân commanded them that they should cut off his head: 'And take you my head, and bear it even unto the White Mount, in London, and bury it there, with the face towards France. And a long time will you be upon the road. In Harlech you will be feasting seven years, the birds of Rhiannon singing unto you the while. And all that time the head will be to you as pleasant company as it ever was when on my body. And at Gwales in Penvro you will be fourscore years, and you may remain there, and the head with you uncorrupted, until you open the door that looks towards Aber Henvelen, and towards Cornwall.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: They cut off his head, and Branwen was the eighth with them; landing at Aber Alaw she looked toward Ireland and toward the Island of the Mighty: 'Alas, woe is me that I was ever born; two islands have been destroyed because of me!' — and there broke her heart, and they made her a four-sided grave on the banks of the Alaw. At Harlech three birds came and sang them a song than which all other songs were unpleasant, seeming far over the sea yet distinct as if close by; and at that repast they continued seven years. Then at Gwales in Penvro they found a fair regal hall with two doors open and the third closed — 'See, yonder, said Manawyddan, is the door that we may not open' — and they remained fourscore years unconscious of any sorrow, in what was called the Entertaining of the noble Head. Not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: One day Heilyn son of Gwynn said: 'Evil betide me, if I do not open the door to know if that is true which is said concerning it.' So he opened the door and looked towards Cornwall and Aber Henvelen — 'And when they had looked, they were as conscious of all the evils they had ever sustained, and of all the friends and companions they had lost, and of all the misery that had befallen them, as if all had happened in that very spot.' They journeyed forth with the head to London and buried it in the White Mount: 'this was the third goodly concealment; and it was the third ill-fated disclosure when it was disinterred, inasmuch as no invasion from across the sea came to this island while the head was in that concealment.' In Ireland none were left alive but five pregnant women, whose five sons divided the land — the five divisions of Ireland. Not verbatim.

narrative.en:
The closing movement of Branwen is a wake that lasts a lifetime — the dead king's head kept alive as company, a hall of forgetting, and the island guarded by a burial.

Brân, wounded in the foot with a poisoned dart, summoned the seven men who had escaped — Pryderi, Manawyddan, Gluneu Eil Taran, Taliesin, Ynawc, Grudyen and Heilyn — and commanded them to cut off his head. 'And take you my head, and bear it even unto the White Mount, in London, and bury it there, with the face towards France. And a long time will you be upon the road. In Harlech you will be feasting seven years, the birds of Rhiannon singing unto you the while. And all that time the head will be to you as pleasant company as it ever was when on my body. And at Gwales in Penvro you will be fourscore years, and you may remain there, and the head with you uncorrupted, until you open the door that looks towards Aber Henvelen, and towards Cornwall.' The dying god inventories the afterlife of his own death: a road of feasts, a hall with a forbidden door, and a grave that outlasts kingdoms.

They cut off his head, and Branwen went the eighth with them. At Aber Alaw in Talebolion she sat down to rest, looked toward Ireland and toward the Island of the Mighty, and said the epitaph of the whole branch: 'Alas, woe is me that I was ever born; two islands have been destroyed because of me!' Then she uttered a loud groan and there broke her heart; and they made her a four-sided grave on the banks of the Alaw — the woman whose suffering had summoned two navies, dying of the arithmetic of it.

At Harlech they stopped to rest and heard that Caswallawn had taken the island — that he had slain six of the seven guardians with a sword invisible under the Veil of Illusion, and Caradawc's heart had broken watching a sword no wielder could be seen. The three birds of Rhiannon came and sang them a song than which all songs they had ever heard were unpleasant in comparison, distant over the sea yet distinct as if close by; and at that repast they stayed seven years. Then they went on to Gwales in Penvro and found a fair regal hall over the ocean, two of its doors open and the third — that which looked toward Cornwall — closed. 'See, yonder,' said Manawyddan, 'is the door that we may not open.' That night they regaled themselves and were joyful; of all the food laid before them and all they had heard, they remembered nothing, neither of that nor of any sorrow whatsoever. There they remained fourscore years, not more weary than when first they came, none knowing the time they had been there, the head no more irksome than if Brân himself had been with them: the Entertaining of the noble Head.

One day Heilyn son of Gwynn said the sentence every otherworld tale waits for: 'Evil betide me, if I do not open the door to know if that is true which is said concerning it.' He opened the door and looked toward Cornwall and Aber Henvelen — and when they had looked, they were as conscious of all the evils they had ever sustained, all the friends and companions they had lost, all the misery that had befallen them, as if it had happened in that very spot. Time had not passed; it had been suspended. They journeyed with the head to London and buried it in the White Mount with the face toward France — 'this was the third goodly concealment; and it was the third ill-fated disclosure when it was disinterred, inasmuch as no invasion from across the sea came to this island while the head was in that concealment.' The head was Britain's guardian: as long as it lay buried, the island could not be invaded from the sea — a talisman doctrine that links the Mabinogi to the Celtic cult of the head, and to the later legend that Arthur's bones stand in the same protection. In Ireland, the tale ends with the five pregnant women who alone survived, whose five sons divided the island into its five provinces — the war's full bill, paid in birth.
narrative.zh: 布蘭溫之結尾是一場持續終生之守靈——死者之頭被存留為伴、一座遺忘之廳、以及以葬禮守衛之島嶼。足中毒鏢之白蘭召集七位倖存者——普里德里、瑪南南、格盧努、塔利埃辛、伊瑙克、格魯迪恩與海林——命他們斬下其首。『攜我之頭至倫敦白丘、面向法蘭西而葬。爾等路上需時甚久。於哈利克你們將宴飲七年、萊安儂之鳥為爾等歌唱；此期間我之頭將如昔日在我身上時一般作愉快之伴。於彭布羅克之格瓦勒斯你們將居八十年，頭與你們同在而不腐，直至你們開啟望向阿伯·亨維倫與康沃爾之門。』垂死之神為自己之死開列來世清單：一條宴飲之路、一座有禁門之廳、一座比王國長久之墳。他們斬下其首；布蘭溫作為第八人同行。於塔萊博利昂之阿伯·阿勞她坐下休息、望向愛爾蘭與巨人島，說出全篇之墓誌銘：『禍哉，我何生於世；兩座島嶼因我而亡！』隨後她大聲呻吟、心碎而亡；眾人於阿勞河岸為她築四方形之墳——其苦難曾召來兩支艦隊的女子，死於這道算術。於哈利克他們歇息，聞知卡薩瓦恩已奪取島國——他以幻象之幔蔽身、以無主之劍殺死七守者中之六人，卡拉多克之心因觀看一柄無持劍者之劍而碎裂。萊安儂之三鳥前來、為他們唱出一首歌，此前所聞一切歌聲與之相比皆為不快；歌聲彷彿遠隔重洋卻清晰如在身旁；他們於此宴中停留七年。繼而至彭布羅克之格瓦勒斯，見臨海之華美王廳、二門開而第三門——望向康沃爾者——緊閉。『看，那邊，』瑪南南曰，『是我們不得開啟之門。』當夜他們自娛而樂；凡所見之食、凡所聞之事，他們一概不復記憶——無論憂傷與否。他們於此居八十年、不比初來時更倦、無人知其居留之久，其頭之不厭猶如白蘭本人同在：尊貴之頭之饗宴。一日海林·格溫之子說出所有彼岸故事等待之句：『若不開門驗證此事真偽，願禍臨我。』他開門望向康沃爾與阿伯·亨維倫——他們一看之下，便同時憶起所曾承受之一切不幸、所失去之一切親友、所遭之一切悲慘，彷彿一切皆發生於此地。時間未曾流逝；時間曾被懸置。他們攜頭赴倫敦、葬於白丘、面向法蘭西——『此為第三次美好之掩藏；而當其被掘出時，是第三次厄運之揭露，蓋其頭埋藏期間，海島未受來自海外之入侵。』其頭乃不列顛之守護者：只要它埋於地下，島嶼便不會被從海上入侵——此護符之說將馬比諾吉與凱爾特頭顱崇拜相連。愛爾蘭一端，故事以五位懷孕婦女之倖存者結束，其五子分島為五省——戰爭之全額帳單，以誕生支付。
